problems.subject: C
problems.explanation: The grazing rule defines a finite directed graph whose unique universal target must be a fixed point. Forum proofs combine congruences for iterates of the doubled/reflected position with increasing 2-adic valuation to rule out other cycles and establish convergence. A late post gives the cleanest route: with k/n in lowest terms, each move keeps the odd part of the denominator and halves its power of 2, so an odd divisor other than 3 yields a second invariant set and hence a second cycle.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: SAS congruence of two triangles built from the parallel and length conditions gives two equal segments; the rotation (spiral similarity of ratio 1) taking one to the other is centred at the major-arc midpoint, which an angle chase places on the circle. Other proofs reflect B, C through the midpoint of AD or use isosceles trapezoids and SAS congruences directly. On the unit circle with the arc midpoint of BC normalised to -1, the parallel-and-equal-length conditions give E and F as closed forms (a real multiple of a chord direction, with the sign fixed by the side condition), and the two distances from -1 to E and F reduce to the moduli of ab+d and a+cd, which are equal because bc = 1.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: The key step is that KL is parallel to AB: as a radical axis of two circles whose centres lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB, or via a cyclic pentagon and a Ceva/Thales ratio argument. Angle chasing then shows that KP and LQ are parallel to sides of the triangle at M, so a homothety at D (or a parallelogram midpoint argument) gives the concurrency. Inversion at M gives alternative proofs of the parallel. A hybrid route: an angle chase first identifies an auxiliary intersection through a spiral similarity at D; barycentric coordinates on the triangle formed by M and the two points on the parallel then parametrize A and B with one free constant, and the meeting point of one of the lines with MD comes out symmetric under swapping the two sides, so the other line passes through it as well.

problems.explanation: Phantom point: take Q on AX with PQ parallel to AB, so Reim makes PQCX cyclic and PQ an external bisector; congruent triangles or a circumcentre-ratio argument then show the same point serves for BY. problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: T lies on the polar of the external-bisector foot, which yields a harmonic range on BC and makes AU, AV isogonal; tangent-length relations and a homothety centred at the internal-bisector foot then place J on the bisector. An alternative proof uses similar triangles and a cyclic quadrilateral centred at J. With the circumcircle as unit circle, J is redefined as the meeting point of OT with the internal bisector; equal distances to BC and TX reduce, after substituting the external-bisector intersection, to a polynomial identity that vanishes. A late forum proof uses Desargues' involution through X and Y, whose fixed harmonic conjugate shows that triangles ABC and AUV share an Apollonius circle, so the two circumcircles are tangent.

Radical axes and a harmonic pencil at X locate the circumcentre as the pole of a chord on PQ; other proofs apply the Miquel inversion at S. With the circumcircle as unit circle and square-root parametrisation of the vertices, S and the arc midpoints have closed forms and P, Q follow from a reality condition on the cyclic quadrilateral through S and the arc midpoint; an affine change of variable reduces the circumcentre-on-line condition to a ratio that is visibly real.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: A spiral similarity at A between triangles ABE and ADC (and their incentres) makes A a Miquel point, putting the intersections of the cross lines with BC on circles through A and I. Radical axes of these circles connect concyclicity of the four incentres with concurrency on AI; one proof finishes with an inversion centred at I. Complex numbers with square-root arc-midpoint parametrisation give all four incentres explicitly; both the concyclicity and the concurrency conditions factor down to the same polynomial equation, once a spurious factor is excluded by the configuration.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Homotheties at the vertices show that corresponding vertices of the two perpendicular-line triangles are collinear with A, B, C, and the three lines meet at a point of the circumcircle. An angle chase puts that point on both circumcircles, and the homothety centred there makes them tangent. With the circumcircle as unit circle and the two parallel lines written as z + conj(z) = t, the intersection points and the vertices of each perpendicular-line triangle are explicit and linear in t, which gives the homothety centre as minus the product of the vertex variables; that centre is then shown to lie on one of the circles by a direct conjugation identity, so the homothety forces tangency.

problems.subject: G
problems.explanation: Monge's theorem reduces the incircle to showing that BB' passes through the exsimilicentre of the two incircles. Reim makes B, I, I', B' concyclic, and the exsimilicentre has equal power with respect to that circle and the circumcircle, by Poncelet arguments or Stewart's theorem. Inverse-power residues modulo d recur by multiplicative periodicity, forcing a return to one and a chain through the target power. Another proof establishes pure periodicity from unique predecessors on the finite orbit and recovers that chain by running backwards.

Read #2 (2023-07-08), VicKmath7 #3 (2023-07-09; edited 2024-06-10), yofro #4, vsamc #5 (2023-07-10), and #6–#9. Added orders/modular periodicity for the central Euler/inverse-power argument in #3/#5; it provides genuine support beyond the existing sequence/size/congruence/process tags. The answer is ceil(log_a d), with d<a^n<ad because gcd(a,d)=1 excludes d being a positive power of a. Bound: start each addition block below d and divide within a-1 additions, so every term is <ad. Sound return-to-one proofs are supplied by #5’s recurring inverse-power residues and #2/#7/#9’s unique-predecessor argument, after the following explicit corrections. In #2 the block contains a multiple of a, not necessarily d. In #3, choose a term immediately after a positive number of divisions whose residue returns to 1; the literal earliest k>1 with x_k=1 mod d can still lie in the initial addition block and need not be a division step. #4’s complete residue system assertion is false: inverse powers visit only the cyclic subgroup generated by a modulo d, which suffices to return to 1. #5’s isolated +a must be +d; #7’s predecessor k+d must be k-d. Reversibility is asserted on the actual bounded orbit, not as a permutation of every integer below ad; gcd(x_k,d)=1 excludes the boundary x_k=d, and the predecessor is ax_k below d or x_k-d above d. Backward powers up to the first a^n>d therefore occur. #6 reports the power a^k where the requested answer is its exponent; #9’s terminal 2^k should read a^k. problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Choose decimal lengths for which the modulus divides a string of nines. Cyclic rotation preserves the multiples and gives every digit position the same distribution. The unit digits repeat in blocks of ten with one extra 9, so its total count exceeds each other nonzero digit count by exactly the chosen length.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2022/IMO2022SL.pdf | PDF pp. 68 (printed pp. 66), Sole solution, cyclic-rotation symmetry and final removal of the all-nines multiple | 2026-10-16 light forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h3107337p28104286; MarkBcc168 #1 statement matched. The cyclic-rotation proof is sound after making the exact-two-values step explicit: choose k a positive multiple of phi(1829), put T=10^k-1, and pad every positive multiple with leading zeroes to length k. Rotation is a permutation of this set and preserves divisibility. Since M=T/1829 satisfies 9M=9 mod 10, M=10q+1; the units sequence is 9,8,...,1,0 repeated, ending with one extra 9. Thus d_1=...=d_8=kq and d_9=k(q+1), exactly two distinct values. This fills the issue raised in #6/#13 and explicitly resolved in #14. T=10^k in #2 has the same multiples since 1829 does not divide 10^k. In #8, d_i=k*f_1 should be d_i=k*f_i. #3’s first modulus should be 10^j, and its digit-swap argument does not justify preservation of the interval [1,T]; it is not used as a complete alternative. #7’s rational rescaling need not give integers, as #10 notes, and is not used. #16’s removal of the all-nines multiple is conditional on an all-equal starting distribution; for the explicit T above, that removal equalizes the counts rather than giving a new working endpoint. problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: The two additive prime-exponent functions give four parity colors, so a five-number set contains a same-color pair. A translated divisibility configuration turns such a pair into consecutive special integers, and bounded overlap among these constructions gives a positive-density bound.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2022/IMO2022SL.pdf | PDF pp. 69 (printed pp. 67), Sole solution; advanced density-paper discussion is not used | 2026-10-16 light forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h3107366p28104497; CyclicISLscelesTrapezoid #1 statement matched; all 11 rendered posts read. TheUltimate123 #3 (2023-07-09) has an invalid displayed configuration: the difference 75 does not divide 5040N; math90 #8 identifies this. It also omits the small-N requirement highlighted by 62861 #6. math90 #7 (2023-07-10; edited 2026-03-06) supplies a sound uniform proof using X_t={72t,72t+6,72t+8,72t+9,72t+12}, after two explicit notation corrections: c=1550 must be c=1/1550, and the same-color pair must satisfy p(a)=p(b) mod 2 and q(a)=q(b) mod 2, not p(a)=q(a),p(b)=q(b). Every pair difference divides both entries; equal parity colors therefore give the consecutive special pair a/(b-a),b/(b-a). Each output is generated at most ten times, since each fixed offset pair determines t uniquely. For N>=100, floor((N-12)/72)>=N/155, so there are at least N/1550 special integers. The t=1 output is <=84 and handles the small-N range. Thus this is a complete adequate forum proof, not merely an asymptotic argument. #10’s proposed density formula is false: for Q equal to all primes, p=q identically and there are no bad numbers, contradicting its claimed density 1. That route and #11’s unspecified constant are not accepted as complete proofs. No external linked problem or density paper was needed. problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Work with the stronger condition allowing a nonnegative quadratic parameter, so deletion remains valid. A quadratic congruence gives the largest prime at most two possible smaller neighbors, and an algebraic identity joins them after deleting it. Induction then uniquely reconstructs the entire cycle whenever it exists.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2022/IMO2022SL.pdf | PDF pp. 71–72 (printed pp. 69–70), Sole solution, both proofs of the quadratic-neighbor lemma and deletion induction; large numerical example not used for tags | 2026-10-16 light forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h2883213p25635143; mathisreaI #1 positive-parameter statement matched. Read lminsl #2, hyay #3, IndoMathXdZ #4, juckter #5, Tintarn #6–#7 and the replies through VicKmath7 #11 (all 2022-07-12). The complete neighbor/deletion/induction arguments corroborate all existing tags. The proof must strengthen the statement to nonnegative (equivalently arbitrary integer) parameters: a deletion may produce zero, while every original positive-parameter arrangement is a special case of this stronger uniqueness theorem. Normalize any integer root via x -> -x-1 before using 0<=x<p. For the largest prime p with neighbors q,r, the normalized roots satisfy x+y=p-1 and x-y=q-r; the quadratic congruence has at most two roots, so those neighbors are forced. Tintarn #6 gives a particularly clean joining identity: set x=q+d,y=r+d, whence p=q+r+2d+1 and qr=d^2+d+k; if d<0 replace it by -d-1. This validates deletion and the induction without requiring a positive new parameter. hyay #3 supplies another complete norm-identity proof. Important transcription limits are explicit: #2’s final normalized expression needs (XY-s)/(2p), not (XY-s)/p, to obtain the odd integer 2u+1. #5’s symmetric expression for k has denominator 4, not 2; its joining step can instead use #6. #4’s integer formulation requires the nonnegative normalization before its size bound. #11’s square-discriminant condition gives a nonnegative root, not always a positive one, so it also needs the strengthened induction. No new substantial method beyond the existing polynomial/congruence/graph/induction/rigidity tags. problems.subject: N
problems.explanation: Quadratic reciprocity, compressed into a Jacobi-symbol calculation, contradicts the proposed exponential congruence. The elementary alternative uses pigeonhole to find a small quadratic-form multiple, descends through factors two, three and five, and finishes with residue obstructions.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2022/IMO2022SL.pdf | PDF pp. 73–74 (printed pp. 71–72), Solutions 1–2 and quadratic-reciprocity comment; Jacobi chain checked visually | 2026-10-16 light forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h3107338p28104291; tastymath75025 #1 corrected statement matched. Read tastymath75025 #2 and DottedCaculator #3 (2023-07-08), brainfertilzer #4 (2023-07-08), VicKmath7 #5 and the early clarifications through megarnie #9 (2023-07-09). The Jacobi proofs in #2/#3/#5 are complete and sound: even n is excluded modulo 3; n=1 fails directly. For odd n>=3, M=2^n+65 is coprime to 15 and M=1 mod 4. Reciprocity gives (5/M)=(M/5)=-1 and (3/M)=(M/3)=1; the proposed congruence and odd exponent would make these symbols equal. #3’s equivalent symbol (15/M) gives the same contradiction. These are Jacobi symbols for a possibly composite denominator; no primality assumption on M is made. #4 supplies another sound implementation via prime divisors: 15 being a quadratic residue forces their classes modulo 60, and hence M’s class, into {1,7,11,17,43,49,53,59}. Writing n=2m+1 then conflicts with 4^m=4 or 16 mod 30 for m>=1; m=0 is the excluded n=1. Thus the explicit residue-class argument also corroborates the existing congruence/QR tags. #6’s historical wording comment does not affect the currently corrected statement. The elementary pigeonhole/descent approach remains supported by the already reviewed official Solution 2; no claim is made to have reviewed a new forum descent proof. No additional substantial method or explanation change. Every existing primary/additional tag, official reference and caveat preserved. problems.explanation: A hypothetical occurrence of every target proportion gives distinct integer hitting times. Monotonic counts of both colors constrain their relative sizes, and choosing maximal earlier times forces one past the allowed range.
problems.notes: https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2020/IMO2020SL.pdf | PDF pp. 38–39 (printed pp. 36–37), Sole solution, hitting-time inequalities and both extremal cases; small-prime sharpness examples read separately | 2026-10-17 light live forum enrichment: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h2625882p22698214; Live vvluo #1 full two-color proportion statement matched (2021-07-20, edited same day). explanation: The points O, A, E, B, M lie on the circle with diameter OM, and E, C, D, M on the circle with diameter EM. subject: G
explanation: The homothety at the tangency point with the circumcircle sends the touch points on CA and CB to the midpoints of the arcs cut off by those sides, so the lines from the tangency point through D and E pass through those arc midpoints. Pascal's theorem on the hexagon formed by the vertices, the arc midpoints and the tangency point then puts I on DE, and since CD = CE with CI the bisector, I is the midpoint. Inversion (centre C or at the incircle) and Casey's theorem give other routes. Let the small circle have radius t and centre P on the bisector of C. The power of P with respect to the circumcircle, computed once from OP and once along the bisector chord through C and the arc midpoint (law of sines for that chord), gives t·cos²(C/2) = 4R·sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2) = r. Then the foot of the bisector on DE is at distance t·cos²(C/2)/sin(C/2) = r/sin(C/2) = CI from C.

subject: G
explanation: The tangency point splits the side into the tangent lengths s − b and s − c of the small triangle, and their reciprocal sum equals the side over the product of the tangent lengths. Heron's formula with the area written as ah/2 and as rs, and r = (s − a)tan(A/2), turn this into 4cot(A/2)/h, where h is the altitude from A. Both triangles share the altitude from A and the angle at A (by the hypothesis), so the two sums agree. Writing the tangent lengths through the inradius and the half-angles at B, at D and at A, each tangent length becomes 2R·sin C·tan(θ) over a sum or difference involving tan(B/2) and tan(θ), where 2θ is the common angle at A. Adding the reciprocals cancels the tan(θ) terms and leaves 1/(R·tanθ·sinA·sinB), which is symmetric in B and C, so the other triangle gives the same value.

subject: G
explanation: Use the Fermat–Torricelli point T. The segments TA, TB, TC make 120° with each other, as do the sides of the equilateral triangle, so each of TA, TB, TC meets the opposite side of DEF at the same angle; splitting ABC into three quadrilaterals with diagonals TA and EF, etc., bounds twice the area by (TA + TB + TC)·DE. The law of cosines with 120° angles and the areas of the three triangles at T give 2(TA + TB + TC)² = a² + b² + c² + 4√3·S; when one angle is at least 120° the same argument works with a signed sum. Equality is attained by the pedal triangle of the isodynamic point.

subject: G
explanation: Write m as twice the area over the longest side. A point inside or on a triangle cannot create a longer side than the triangle's longest side, and a point on a side gives a sub-triangle with no larger m (scaling by a parallel). Then split by position of X: inside the triangle, add the three areas over the common bound; when a vertex lies inside the triangle of X and the other two, or the four points are convex, shrink to sub-triangles through the intersection of the diagonals and reduce to the first case.

subject: G
explanation: A circle with centre P bisects a circle with centre A exactly when A lies on their radical axis, i.e. r² = PA² + r_A². For two of the circles this forces PB² − PA² to be a constant, so the admissible centres form a fixed line perpendicular to AB. For non-collinear centres two such lines meet in exactly one point; for collinear centres the lines are parallel to each other (no circle) or coincide, and then every admissible circle meets the line of centres at the same two points, found from the power of A and B.

subject: G
explanation: Invert at A. The angle condition becomes a right angle at the image of B in the image triangle, and the length condition becomes equality of the two legs at that vertex, so the image triangle is an isosceles right triangle; the required ratio is its hypotenuse over a leg, √2. The circle through A, C, D becomes the line through the images of C and D, which is a diameter of the image of the other circle, so the circles are orthogonal (equivalently, the angles at A and B subtending CD add up to 90°). A spiral similarity at B produces the same isosceles right triangle without inversion. With complex coordinates, the quotient (b − d)(a − c)/((a − d)(b − c)) has modulus 1 by the length condition and argument 90° by the angle condition (C and D on the same side), so it equals i. The identity (a − b)(c − d) = (a − c)(b − d) − (a − d)(b − c) then gives (a − b)(c − d) = (i − 1)(a − d)(b − c), so the ratio is |i − 1| = √2. Orthogonality is handled by the angle chase (hybrid).

subject: G
explanation: A quarter-turn about a vertex of the quadrilateral maps each side line of the first quadrilateral to the corresponding side line of the second, and the same quarter-turn is obtained about any point of the bisector of the right angle where those two lines meet. That bisector passes through the vertex and through the apex of the isosceles right triangle erected on the opposite diagonal (a cyclic quadrilateral with two right angles). Because the diagonals are perpendicular, the two squares built on the diagonals have parallel sides, so they are homothetic and the four bisectors concur at the centre of homothety; one quarter-turn about that point maps one quadrilateral onto the other.

subject: G
explanation: Two segments joining opposite centres are perpendicular exactly when the sums of squares of opposite sides of the centre quadrilateral agree. subject: G
explanation: By the Erdős–Mordell inequality the distances from P to the vertices sum to at least twice the distances to the sides, so for some vertex the distance to the vertex is at least twice the distance to the adjacent side; the corresponding angle then has sine at most 1/2, and the case of an angle of at least 150° makes another of the three angles small. Alternatively, the law of cosines in the three sub-triangles and the area split give a² + b² + c² < 4√3·[ABC], contradicting Weitzenböck's inequality. If all three angles exceeded 30°, trigonometric Ceva would make the product of the sines of the other three angles at the vertices exceed 1/8, so the product of all six sines exceeds 1/64. The six angles sum to 180°, and concavity of log sin (Jensen) bounds that product by sin⁶30° = 1/64, a contradiction.

subject: G
explanation: The angle bisector theorem applied twice (in the whole triangle and in a sub-triangle) gives AI/AA′ = (b+c)/(a+b+c), so the ratio equals (a+b)(b+c)(c+a)/(a+b+c)³. The upper bound is AM–GM on the three sums, and the strict lower bound follows from the Ravi substitution, where the product exceeds twice the cube of the semiperimeter. In areal (barycentric) coordinates with I = (p, q, r), AI/AA′ equals 1 − p = q + r, so the ratio is (p+q)(q+r)(r+p); AM–GM gives the upper bound for any interior point, and substituting the incenter (a : b : c) reduces the lower bound to the same algebraic inequality.

Then the segments joining midpoints of opposite edges are common perpendicular bisectors meeting at their common midpoint, which is equidistant from the vertices and so is O; the midpoint quadrilaterals are rhombi (their sides are halves of equal opposite edges), and the required angles are the right angles between rhombus diagonals.

subject: G
explanation: A solid-geometry problem. The part containing the apex is a cone over the elliptical section, so its volume is one third of the ellipse area times the apex-to-plane distance. In the axial cross-section the major axis is a side of a triangle with the apex, and the Dandelin spheres appear as the incircle and excircle of that triangle, so the focal distance (and hence the minor axis) comes from tangent lengths; the ratio is 1/(3√3). Coordinates in the axial plane give the far end of the major axis and the foot of the perpendicular from the apex as intersections of explicit lines, yielding the major axis and the apex-to-plane distance; combined with the Dandelin-sphere step for the minor axis this gives the volume ratio.

subject: G
explanation: Alternate angles make the triangles cut off by the parallel line isosceles, so CG = CB and CE = CA, and the parallel gives GF/FB = CB/AB and DE/DA = CA/AB. If CB > CA then the bisector segment BG exceeds AE, so FB > DA, and multiplying the two strict inequalities forces GF > DE, a contradiction; by symmetry CA = CB. The law of sines in the two small triangles at C, with the angle-bisector lengths CF and CD, turns GF = DE into (a+c)b/((b+c)a) = sin(A/2)/sin(B/2); assuming a ≥ b the right side is at least 1, which forces b ≥ a.

subject: G
explanation: The diagonals must meet at the A-Dumpty point. Take the spiral similarity at that point sending CA to AB; applied to a pair of opposite vertices and their midpoint it produces cyclic quadrilaterals and a directly similar triangle, which shows that a midpoint other than the Dumpty point determines the whole diagonal line. Two diagonals sharing such a midpoint would coincide, so the common midpoint is the Dumpty point, which lies on circle BOC. With the parallelogram centre as origin, the two angle conditions say two quotients are real; subtracting them shows that unless bc equals a squared the vertex X has a fixed argument, and the same for Y, which would make the parallelogram degenerate. So bc = a^2, i.e. the centre is the Dumpty point.

subject: C
explanation: Assume all cycle lengths differ and take a DFS tree: each of the k extra edges closes a cycle with a tree path, these lengths are distinct, so they sum to about k²/2. Double counting extra edges that jump over each vertex gives a vertex jumped by about k²/(2n) of them, while every pair of such edges forms a different cycle and there are at most n cycles; hence k = O(n^(3/4)).

explanation: Q(x) = x^d with p ≡ 1 (mod d) takes only 1+(p−1)/d values, which rules out c < d. subject: G
explanation: Invert in the fixed circle Gamma: the vertices become midpoints of the sides of the triangle formed by the fixed contact point and the two moving contact points, so the circumcircle becomes a nine-point circle of a triangle inscribed in Gamma. Its radius is fixed, and the centroid homothety along the Euler line moves its centre on a fixed circle, so it is tangent to two fixed concentric circles; invert back. With Gamma the unit circle and the fixed tangent as a vertical line, the circumcircle has an explicit equation in terms of the moving point; the substitution t -> 1/t turns it into a circle of radius 1/2 whose centre is an affine image of 1/x, so as the point runs over a circle the image circles stay tangent to two fixed circles.

subject: C
explanation: The answer is 2n−2, attained by all (n−1)-subsets with n−2 singletons. For the bound induct on n, merging elements that no set separates; otherwise the sets avoiding the least frequent element cover the rest and are not tight, so some element lies in exactly one of them, and deleting that set and at most one other makes two elements inseparable, so merging finishes.

subject: G
explanation: Treat each parabola as a conic tangent to the line at infinity at the vertical direction; Pascal (or a harmonic projection) shows the two tangent intersections lie on the vertical line through the midpoint of the common chord. If that line were not perpendicular to the chord, comparing the two pairs of opposite tangent lengths contradicts Pitot's condition, so it is the common axis. Direct coordinates: the tangents at two points of a parabola with vertical axis meet above the midpoint of the chord, so both tangent intersections share that x-coordinate; tangent-length equality from the incircle plus the law of cosines then forces the chord to be horizontal.

explanation: λ is completely multiplicative and +1 on squares. explanation: C_n = (n−1)/(2n). subject: G
explanation: Assume one concurrence. Monge–d'Alembert applied to an auxiliary circle tangent to two of the four circles identifies it and shows it is also tangent at the given point; a tangent-length chase then shows the other two points are midpoints of common tangents, hence on the radical axis of the remaining pair, and the radical axis theorem gives the second concurrence. By the law of sines (area ratios), each collinearity is equivalent to a product of ratios equalling 1; right-triangle similarities express the ratios through the radii, and the two products turn out identical.

subject: A
explanation: Colour each monomial by the set of variables it actually contains. Every 0/1 substitution kills f, because the product contains the factor x1+…+xn−|S|; so for each set S the colour sums over the nonempty subsets of S add to zero, and induction on |S| (Möbius inversion, or: a multilinear polynomial vanishing on the cube is zero) makes each colour sum vanish. subject: N
explanation: A term is −1 exactly when the short interval ((a−1)k/p, ak/p) contains an integer; call such k bad. Bad indices are closed under addition. After absorbing bad indices into b one may assume b+1 is good or b = p−1, and then each pair {k, b+1−k} contains a good index, so good terms are at least half. Alternatively, the bad k up to c are lattice points of a thin triangle, bounded by Pick's theorem.

subject: C
explanation: Assume every area-1 rectangle has a point inside. By induction on n, for every ε > 0 some region of area below ε (an ellipse, or a triangle) contains n points: an area-preserving affine map makes the current small region round, an area-1 rectangle placed just beside it must contain a new point, and a slightly larger region of still tiny area covers both. A rectangle of comparable area around a region with 2026 points has area below 1, and enlarging it to area 1 gives more than 2025 points.

subject: C
explanation: The answer is α = 3/2: a k×k block of red points has about k³ total label, so α ≥ 3/2. For the bound, a label is at most the number of red points in its row and at most the number in its column. In a row with r red points the labels therefore sum to at most min(r², n) ≤ r√n, and summing over rows gives n^(3/2). Equivalently, bound each label by the geometric mean of its row and column counts and apply Cauchy–Schwarz.

subject: G
explanation: The common tangents meet BC at X and Y with M the midpoint of XY (angle chase through the midpoints of the tangent segments, or Desargues' involution), so the centre Z of ω is the arc midpoint of XY on the bisector of angle XTY at the exsimilicentre T. The line TZ is the line of centres, i.e. the perpendicular bisector of AM. An inversion at T swapping the two circles gives angle ZTA, which matches the angle at the arc midpoint W of BC, so A, Z, W, T are concyclic; the radical axis theorem for this circle, ω and Γ finishes. With T at the origin and the tangents y = ±kx, put X = (a, ka), Y = (b, −kb). Equal tangent lengths from points of BC force M to be the midpoint of XY; then the circumcentre, the arc midpoint, the point on the bisector and on the perpendicular bisector of AM, and the circle ω all get explicit coordinates, and the two powers of that point come out equal.

subject: N
explanation: Modulo a prime p, a³+b³+abc ≡ 0 has only p²−p+1 solutions (one c for each pair with ab ≢ 0, plus a ≡ b ≡ 0), a proportion below 1. Take many primes not dividing the common difference with the product of these proportions tiny. By the CRT, triples up to PN whose value is divisible by P = p1⋯pk are rare, while the progression contains a fixed proportion of multiples of P; since a ≥ b ≥ c keeps a, b, c below the cube root of the value, counting gives a contradiction.

subject: C
explanation: The answer is 171 = 83 + 89 − 1. Ana's integers must cover every residue class modulo all but at most one candidate prime, or two indicator functions fool her. For the two largest remaining primes p and q, join two chosen integers when they agree modulo p or modulo q; replacing each clique by a path shows the graph has at most n − 2 edges when n ≤ p + q − 2, so it is disconnected, and colouring its components gives functions of two different periods with the same values. Conversely, 171 consecutive multiples of 97 work, since the graph on 171 indices joining differences 83 and 89 is a tree.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2025.pdf — Solution to TST 1 (Anthony Wang), read in full: residue-coverage claim, edge-count disconnection, acyclic difference graph for the construction. subject: A
explanation: Let r, s, t be the roots of λ³ − a1λ² + b1λ − 1, so rst = 1. By Vieta and induction, a_n and b_n are the power sums of r, s, t and of their reciprocals with exponent 2^(n−1): squaring a power sum and subtracting twice the pairwise products, which are reciprocals because rst = 1, doubles the exponent. Since a1 > b1 the cubic is negative at 1, so it has a real root r > 1. If all roots are real the root of largest modulus dominates; if two are complex conjugates they have modulus below 1, so a_n stays within 2 of a fast-growing power of r. Either way a_n is eventually increasing.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2025.pdf — Solution to TST 2 (Holden Mui), read in full: power-sum representation via Vieta, real-root and complex-root cases. Live AoPS checked 2026-11-17 (Claude Code, via the user's Chrome): https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h3462250p33455233; posts read #1–#17 of 17 (all loaded). #2 john0512 (most thanked), #7 peace09, #12, #13 ray66 and #14 HamstPan38825 use the same cubic-roots representation; #4 DottedCaculator and #6 asbodke give an elementary split into the cases a1 + b1 < −2 and ≥ −2 (not tagged separately); #8 notes a 2006 Belarus precursor.

subject: G
explanation: P and Q are isogonal conjugates in the polygon. The reflections of P in the sides form a polygon whose vertices are equidistant from Q (the line from each vertex to Q is the perpendicular bisector of two consecutive reflections), so it is cyclic. Each circumcentre step preserves the angles that P makes with consecutive vertices, so after n steps the polygon is spirally similar about P to the reflected one, proving (a). The rotation angles of the spiral similarities at P and Q are opposite and their law-of-sines scale factors coincide because the angle condition swaps the sines, so P, Q, O_Q, O_P form an isosceles trapezoid, proving (b).
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2025.pdf — Solution to TST 3 (Ruben Carpenter), read in full. subject: G
explanation: Since AY = AZ and reflection in a side through A preserves distances from A, the points Y, Z, Y′, Z′ lie on a circle centred at A, so the circumcentre S of X′Y′Z′ has AS ⊥ Y′Z′, and similarly BS ⊥ Z′X′, CS ⊥ X′Y′. Writing the direction of Y′Z′ through the reflections of the common line in CA and AB and subtracting the analogous expression for Z′X′ gives ∠ASB = ∠ACB, so S lies on the circumcircle. (The author's solution instead identifies S through the anticomplementary triangle and a Steiner line.) With the circumcircle as unit circle and the line given by Re(z/δ) = λ, the projection of A onto the line is the midpoint of YZ, so X, Y, Z come from the three projections. Reflecting X in BC gives X′, and adding abc/δ² to it gives an expression symmetric in a, b, c, so X′, Y′, Z′ are equidistant from −abc/δ², a point of the unit circle.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2025.pdf — Solutions to TST 4 (Michael Ren), both read in full. subject: C
explanation: Let π send each pad to the destination of its jump; it has exactly two cycles. The jumps cover 2025ℓ positions in total, so the average jump is ℓ ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}, and ℓ = 2 or 5 makes π a single translation with one or five cycles. For ℓ = 3 or 4, subtract ℓ from every jump: the cycles of the shifted permutation have zero net displacement, which forces short cycles of a few explicit types on consecutive pads. Following three or four auxiliary frogs through these blocks shows how they are permuted; only ℓ = 4 with the frogs' paths pairing up gives exactly two cycles, and then each frog makes two laps.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2025.pdf — Solution to TST 5 (Linus Tang), read in full: average-jump bound, classification of zero-displacement cycles, auxiliary frogs and permutation parity. Statement brute-forced for odd n from 7 to 25 (check_2025_5.py).

subject: N
explanation: Work with polynomials first: by the Chinese remainder theorem in Q[x], each choice of signs gives a polynomial f of degree at most 23 with f ≡ ±cx modulo c²x² + 1 for c = 1, …, 12, so every f² + 1 is divisible by the degree-24 product of these quadratics. Clearing denominators and evaluating at large multiples of a fixed integer gives 2025 integers whose squares plus one share a factor of size about x^24, while the integers themselves are only about x^23, so any ε below 1/23 works. A purely integer construction with primes ≡ 1 (mod 4), Hensel lifting and the CRT also works.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2025.pdf — Solutions to TST 6 (Pitchayut Saengrungkongka), read in full: Solution 1 polynomial CRT, Solution 2 an explicit coprime polynomial sequence in Z[x], Solutions 3–4 cyclotomic-type constructions (Solution 3 uses Zsigmondy; not tagged). Live AoPS checked 2026-11-17 (Claude Code, via the user's Chrome): https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h3477769p33692821; posts read #1–#14 of 14 (all loaded). #2 DottedCaculator and #14 HamstPan38825 complete polynomial-CRT proofs (same as official Solution 1); #7 thevictor complete integer construction via Hensel lifting and CRT (its key identity checked by hand); #3 author, #5 asbodke other constructions; #10 YaoAOPS reports an earlier wrong attempt.

subject: A
explanation: The answer is C = 3/2: one a_i just below 2 and many equal large a_i force the reciprocal sum to be either at most 1 or close to 3/2. For the bound, start with every b_i equal to the ceiling (sum below 1) and switch them to floors one at a time; the sum rises monotonically to above 1, and each switch adds 1/(m(m+1)) ≤ 1/2, so the first time it exceeds 1 it is still below 3/2. Alternatively, if some a_i < 2 use b_i = 1 and ceilings elsewhere, and otherwise floors lose at most a factor 3/2.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2024.pdf — Solution to TST 2024/1 (Merlijn Staps), read in full: lower-bound family, one-at-a-time switching argument, and an alternate case split. Live AoPS checked 2026-11-18 (Claude Code, via the user's Chrome): https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h3214877p29409075; posts read #1–#41 of 41 (all loaded). #2 megarnie, #3 CT17, #12 MathLuis, #16 VicKmath7, #36 KevinYang2.71 and the late #38–#41 use the same switching or case-split arguments; #7 also gives the fixed-n answer (3n−2)/(2n−1); #6 a wrong answer 4/3. Nothing new in the tail.

subject: G
explanation: An angle chase reduces the claim to BP = BQ, i.e. to the line PQ making a fixed angle with AP. Restated with D as the incentre of an isosceles triangle AEF, let U be where BD meets EF and V where BI meets the circumcircle: the circle on diameter AB and a cyclic quadrilateral through B, E, U, V put P, U, V on a line, the tangency makes APUQ cyclic, and D being the orthocentre of AUF gives PQ parallel to DF, the required direction. The author's route: the perpendicularity BD ⟂ AC becomes the identity sin(B/2) = sin|A/2 − C/2| / cos(A/2) via the law of sines in triangle BDI; the law of sines in ABQ (with the tangency angle) and the right triangle APB then give the same expression for BQ and BP, and a short angle chase finishes.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2024.pdf — Solutions to TST 2024/2, all three read in full. subject: C
explanation: Encode the subset sums in the generating function P(x) = Σ x^(sum of S) over k-subsets. Since p divides C(n, k), Legendre's formula (or Lucas) gives a power p^r with n mod p^r < k mod p^r, and then the cyclotomic polynomial Φ_{p^r} divides P: either from the q-binomial product formula, or by substituting a primitive p^r-th root of unity into Π(1 + x^i y) and seeing that the y^k coefficient vanishes. Divisibility by Φ_{p^r} means the counts of sums in residues j, j + p^(r−1), … modulo p^r are equal, so grouping residues by their block gives p equal classes.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2024.pdf — Solution to TST 2024/3 (Ankan Bhattacharya), read in full: Legendre, cyclotomic divisibility proved two ways (q-binomial; roots of unity in Π(1 + x^i y)). subject: C
explanation: Only even n work: alternate the P's between two points slightly more than 1 apart and the Q's between two points on the perpendicular diameter, then perturb. For odd n, show that two points within distance 1 of both P1 and P2 and on the same side of line P1P2 are less than 1 apart (triangle inequality on the crossing diagonals of a convex quadrilateral, or an obtuse angle when one point is inside the triangle). Hence consecutive Q's lie on opposite sides of P1P2, which is impossible around an odd cycle.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2024.pdf — Solution to TST 2024/4 (Ray Li), read in full: perturbed construction, two-case lemma (convex quadrilateral / point inside triangle), parity. subject: N
explanation: The answer is 11, from 1, 2, …, 2024 and the powers of 2. In an arithmetic progression of 2024 terms (after removing a common factor), ν_p of the terms takes at most ⌊log_p 2023⌋ + 2 values, because only one term can have valuation above that of every index difference. Common terms with a geometric sequence have pairwise different ν_p for any prime p dividing the ratio, so an odd prime gives at most 8. If the ratio is a power of 2 the bound is 12, and the twelfth term is excluded because the progression, containing the odd term b and 2b, cannot reach 2^11·b.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2024.pdf — Solution to TST 2024/5 (Ray Li), read in full: ν_p lemma for arithmetic progressions, odd-prime and power-of-2 cases, final size argument. subject: A
explanation: The solutions are the constants and f(x) = x + 1. The engine is that a nonconstant solution has no nonzero period: substituting y + d for y shows f(dx) = f(0). Comparing two substitutions gives the symmetry f(f(x) + y) = f(f(y) + x), and iterating it shows any defect in f(f(x) + y) = f(x) + f(y) would be a period. Then f(0) = 1 and f(x + 1) = f(x) + 1, which upgrade to f(x + y) + 1 = f(x) + f(y), and one more application of the no-period principle forces f(x) = x + 1.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2024.pdf — Solution to TST 2024/6 (Milan Haiman), read in full: no-period lemma, symmetry, Cauchy-type relation, f = x + 1. Live AoPS checked 2026-11-18 (Claude Code, via the user's Chrome): https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h3234860p29642897; posts read #1–#30 of 30 (all loaded). #2 CT17, #3 DottedCaculator, #4 megarnie, #5 i3435, #7 CircleInvert, #8 YaoAOPS, #11 Supercali, #21 hung9A, #23 vsamc and late #26–#30 complete substitution proofs, most via the same aperiodicity idea; #15 notes a similar earlier problem.

subject: C
explanation: With 2n points the maximum is 2n² − 2n + 2, reached by alternating hops of lengths n and n − 1 with one adjustment. For the bound, draw the n diameters through the midpoints between adjacent points: a hop's length is the number of diameters it crosses, every diameter is crossed an even number of times because the tour is closed, and at most one diameter can be crossed by every hop (two such diameters would leave whole arcs unvisited). Summing crossings gives the bound. Alternatively, pair consecutive hops and compare with the tour through the odd-indexed points.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2023.pdf — Solution to TST 2023/1 (Kevin Cong), read in full: construction, pairing bound, and diameter-crossing parity bound. Live AoPS checked 2026-11-18 (Claude Code, via the user's Chrome): https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h2977026p26685816; posts read #1–#31 of 31 (all loaded). #5 squareman, #6 magicarrow (most thanked), #15 SHZhang, #16, #21–#31 complete proofs with the diameter or pairing count; #8 IAmTheHazard induction proof (not relied on); #7 notes it was also EGMO TST 2023/1.

subject: G
explanation: Invert in the circle on diameter BC: the circles BME and CMF become the lines BE and CF, the common tangents become the two circles through M tangent to both lines, and K goes to their second intersection, which is the reflection of M in the bisector of angle BHC, so HK* is a symmedian of BHC. K on the circumcircle means K* lies on circle BHC, making (H, K*; B, C) harmonic, so BC bisects angle HMK and K is the reflection of H in BC, i.e. AK ⟂ BC. Other official proofs use the Miquel point Q of BCEF and show QBKC is harmonic. With the circumcircle as unit circle, compute the Miquel point Q, the centres O1, O2 of circles BME and CMF and the point T = −bc/a on the altitude. Q, M and T all have the same distance ratio to O1 and O2, equal to the ratio of the radii, which is also K's ratio since K is the exsimilicentre; so Q, M, T, K lie on one Apollonian circle, and K on the circumcircle forces K = T.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2023.pdf — Solutions to TST 2023/2, all five read in full. subject: C
explanation: Writing 300 = s(s+1)/2 with s = 24 and k = 20, the answer is ks(ks+1)/2 = 115440, from f(n) = max(s − n, 0) and g(n) = max(ks − n, 0). For the bound take g as large as allowed; then the complement of g's Young diagram is the k-fold sumset of the complement of f's, a description symmetric under reflecting the diagrams in the diagonal, so f and g may be replaced by their conjugate partitions. Three estimates follow — Hermite's identity bounding g by f at floors of n/k, the same for the conjugates, and a direct count using where f vanishes — and in every case one of them gives the bound.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2023.pdf — Solution to TST 2023/3 (Sean Li), read in full: construction, Young-diagram sumset and conjugation symmetry, three bounds. Live AoPS checked 2026-11-18 (Claude Code, via the user's Chrome): https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h2976989p26685437; posts read #1–#19 of 19 (all loaded). #10 DottedCaculator (most thanked), #12 Afternonz, #16 Leo.Euler (grid version), #18 YaoAOPS and #19 KevinYang2.71 complete proofs along these lines; #8–#11 discuss whether it is algebra or combinatorics.

subject: N
explanation: The map x ↦ x ⊕ ax is injective exactly for even a. If 2^k exactly divides a, the last k bits of x ⊕ ax are those of x, which determine k more bits of ax and hence the next k bits of x, and so on up the binary expansion. If a is odd, take x = 2^n − 1 and y = 2^n + 1 with 2^n > a: both x ⊕ ax and y ⊕ ay equal the n-bit string of a − 1 written twice.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2023.pdf — Solution to TST 2023/4 (Carl Schildkraut), read in full: bit-by-bit recovery for even a, explicit collision for odd a. subject: C
explanation: If gcd(m, n) = d > 1, labellings with all 1×d sums zero are valid, so every row needs a question and no finite number suffices. If gcd(m, n) = 1 the answer is (m−1)² + (n−1)²: labellings with zero m-sums along rows and columns form a space of dimension (m−1)², similarly for n, and they meet only in zero, giving the lower bound. For the upper bound, valid labellings are mn-periodic (Chicken McNugget), so they are polynomials modulo x^mn − 1 and y^mn − 1, and evaluating at pairs of mn-th roots of unity shows at most (m−1)² + (n−1)² evaluations can be nonzero, bounding the dimension.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2023.pdf — Solutions to TST 2023/5 (Nikolai Beluhov), read in full: dimension lower bound; generating functions with roots of unity (Ankan Bhattacharya); explicit questioning algorithm with a gcd induction lemma (author). subject: A
explanation: Suppose |Δ| ≤ N. Then f is injective, so its arrow graph n → f(n) is a union of chains and cycles. Boundedness rules out cycles (iterates would collide), allows at most 2N + 1 chains, and then shows there is a single half-infinite chain, so every integer is f^k(c) for a starting point c. In the index g(k) = f^k(c) the condition says g(x) − x is injective and |g(g(b+1)+a) − g(g(a+1)+b)| ≤ N; since g is a bijection, g(x) − x is unbounded below, and choosing B with g(B) far below B forces infinitely many values of B − g(B) into a bounded window, a contradiction.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2023.pdf — Solution to TST 2023/6 (Maxim Li), read in full: injectivity, arrow-graph structure (no cycles, finitely many chains, one chain), reindexing and final counting. subject: N
explanation: Exactly the composite s work. If s = (w + x)(y + z), the products a = wy, b = wz, c = xy, d = xz make the symmetric sum equal to wxyz·s. Conversely, since d ≡ −(a + b + c) modulo s, the condition rearranges to s dividing (a + b)(a + c)(a + d), a product of positive integers smaller than s, which a prime cannot divide.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2021.pdf — Solution to TST 2021/1 (Ankan Bhattacharya, Michael Ren), read in full: factorised construction, product identity for primes, and a remark using an even polynomial over F_s. subject: G
explanation: The fixed point is K = AF ∩ BE, where AE and BF are the chords of Γ parallel to the two given lines. For X = AC ∩ BD, the powers of any point with respect to circles XAB, XCD, XAD, XBC satisfy pow(XAB) + pow(XCD) = pow(XAD) + pow(XBC), because the difference is linear and vanishes at A, B, C, D. By Reim's theorem circles XAD and XBC pass through fixed points on AF and BE, so K's power with respect to each of them is a fixed product, and so is its power to Γ; hence its power to circle XCD is fixed. The authors instead show K lies on every radical axis using Reim and Pascal. Using that the difference of powers with respect to circle XCD and Γ is a linear function of the point, evaluate it at D and at L = AX ∩ DK and interpolate to K; the law of sines turns the result into (AK·β + BK·α)/sin∠AXB, where α and β are the fixed distances from the two given lines to the parallel chords, and ∠AXB is fixed on the arc.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2021.pdf — Solutions to TST 2021/2 (Andrew Gu, Frank Han), both approaches read in full. subject: A
explanation: The solutions are the concave quadratics ay² + by + c with a ≤ 0. The condition says the slope of each chord is a supergradient (a tangent-line bound) at the chord's midpoint; this makes f concave and hence continuous. Comparing the inequality at nearby symmetric points shows the one-sided slopes at any point converge, so the supergradient is unique; two chords with the same midpoint then have equal slopes, giving the third-difference identity f(x+3d) − 3f(x+2d) + 3f(x+d) − f(x) = 0. So f is quadratic on each lattice (1/n)Z, the quadratics agree, and continuity finishes.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2021.pdf — Solution to TST 2021/3 (Gabriel Carroll), read in full: supergradient reformulation, concavity and continuity, uniqueness of supergradients, third differences; remark with a differentiability finish (Michael Ren). subject: A
explanation: The possible values are exactly 0 ≤ r ≤ 1/2. Induction with strict decrease and integrality gives b_n ≤ n(n+1)/2, so the ratios b_n/n² stay at most 1/2 + 1/(2n) and r ≤ 1/2; r = 0 and r = 1/2 come from b_n = 1 and b_n = n(n+1)/2. For 0 < r < 1/2, start with the triangular numbers and switch to b_n = ⌈rn² + n⌉ from some point on: the extra +n keeps the ratios strictly decreasing despite the ceiling, and they tend to r.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2020.pdf — Solution to TST 2020/1 (Carl Schildkraut, Milan Haiman), read in full: greedy induction bound and explicit construction (Nikolai Beluhov). subject: G
explanation: Invert at T swapping the two circles; it sends A, B, C, D to points E, F, V, W. T and Y both lie on the radical axis of circles ADE and BCF (equal tangent-style products from T, and YA·YD = YB·YC). X also has equal power: X lies on lines VE and FW by radical axes with the two given circles, making it the centre of a negative inversion between circles ADE and BCF, which are congruent (equal chords AE = BF and supplementary inscribed angles). So T, X, Y lie on one radical axis. A projective route chases cross-ratios through the inversion at T. Similar triangles YAC and YBD give d(Y, AC)/d(Y, BD) = AC/BD. For T, the distances to AC and BD are TA·sin and TB·sin of the angles these chords make with the tangents, and since TA/TB = r1/r2 and a chord equals the diameter times the sine of its tangent–chord angle, the ratio is also AC/BD. Both T and Y lie inside the same angle at X, so they are on one line through X.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2020.pdf — Solutions to TST 2020/2, all four read in full. subject: C
explanation: Hephaestus wins exactly for α > 2. With α > 2 he first walls off one side of the (diamond-shaped) flood, keeps lengthening that wall while the water spreads sideways, then closes two side walls at once and finally the far side, the slack α − 2 paying for each sudden addition. For α = 2, follow a shortest flooding path c0, …, cn of cells; it is an induced path, so its boundary has 2n + 4 edges, and shining a ray from each cell toward each boundary edge hits distinct walls of the closed levee, so at least 2n + 4 walls are needed after n + 1 turns.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2020.pdf — Solution to TST 2020/3 (Nikolai Beluhov), read in full: rectangle strategy for α > 2, path-and-laser counting for α = 2. subject: C
explanation: Triangles of G survive in G', and a vertex of degree at least 3 with two non-adjacent neighbours creates a new triangle, so if G is isomorphic to G'' no such vertex exists and every component is a clique, a cycle or a path. Isolated vertices, odd cycles and cliques of size at least 3 are fixed by the operation, while even cycles and paths split into more components, which can never merge back; so G consists only of fixed components and G ≅ G'.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2020.pdf — Solution to TST 2020/4 (Zack Chroman, Mehtaab Sawhney), read in full: triangle count monovariant, classification of components, component count. subject: N
explanation: Such P exists exactly when some prime p divides n while a smaller prime does not (rad n is not a primorial). The first time an iterate of 0 vanishes modulo n is the lcm of the same quantity modulo each prime power, by the CRT. Modulo p^e it has only prime factors at most p: by induction, after reaching 0 modulo p^(e−1), the further iterates stay among the p multiples of p^(e−1). For the construction, an interpolation polynomial over Z/p^e cycles 0 → 1 → … → k−1 → 0 for any k < p, and P ≡ x elsewhere glues these by the CRT.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2020.pdf — Solution to TST 2020/5 (Carl Schildkraut), read in full: zero-order lcm over prime powers, pigeonhole induction, interpolation construction. Live AoPS checked 2026-11-18 (Claude Code, via the user's Chrome): https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h1994655p13913769; posts read #1–#36 of 36 (all loaded). #2 MarkBcc168, #3 spartacle, #4 IndoMathXdZ, #7, #8, #9 amuthup, #10 Eyed, #13, #14 squareman, #15 megarnie, #19, #21 GrantStar, #22 starchan and late #30–#36 complete proofs; #28 notes Lagrange interpolation suffices.

subject: G
explanation: Let K_i be the foot from P to P_{i−1}P_{i+1}; equal products PP_i·PK_i show by inversion at P that the K_i are concyclic. Reflecting P in the centre of that circle gives a point E with matching perpendicular feet E_i. Using the orthocentres H_i of triangles P P_i P_{i+1}, Reim's theorem and an isogonality, E, Q_i and E_i are collinear, and the triangles EQ_iQ_{i+1} and PK_iK_{i+1} have parallel sides; so the Q-polygon is homothetic to the concyclic K-polygon. A generalisation uses P and the circumcentre as isogonal conjugates and a power-ratio circle. With the circumcircle as unit circle, the perpendicularity conditions say the dot products PP_j·PP_{j+1} equal a constant k. Neighbours of a vertex c are then the roots of an explicit quadratic, so by Vieta each Q_i comes out as ((c − p) + f(p + c))/(c·p̄ − 1) with f depending only on p and k. As c runs over the unit circle this is a Möbius image of a circle, so all Q_i lie on one fixed circle.
notes: Official solutions: https://web.evanchen.cc/exams/sols-TST-IMO-2020.pdf — Solutions to TST 2020/6, both read in full.
